name: Graham
who: Retired electrician. Lives with his wife. Brother had a heart attack at 70.
opening: "Just my blood pressure script, doc."

actions.label: Side effects?
actions.text: No problems with the tablets. Takes them every morning.

actions.label: Ask about his golf handicap and weekend plans
actions.text: Plays off 18. Off to the coast for the weekend.
actions.why: Friendly, but it eats minutes and changes nothing.

actions.label: Smoking
actions.text: Ex-smoker. Quit 10 years ago after 30 years.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks his blood pressure is "sorted". Quietly worried about his brother's heart attack. Expects a script and the car park.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "Oh, and by the way, I get a bit tight in the chest walking up the hill to the shops. Goes away when I stop."
actions.why: "Anything else?" was where the angina was hiding.

actions.label: Chest tightness: tell me more
actions.text: Central tightness on exertion for about 6 weeks. Eases within a few minutes of resting. Never at rest. None today.
actions.why: Characterising exertional chest pain is the whole consult once it's mentioned.

actions.label: Blood pressure
actions.text: 142/86. Pulse 78, regular.

actions.label: Heart, lungs, ankles
actions.text: Normal heart sounds, clear chest, no ankle swelling.

actions.label: Order a chest X-ray
actions.text: Requested.
actions.why: A chest X-ray doesn't help assess exertional chest pain.

actions.label: ECG
actions.text: Sinus rhythm, no acute changes. A normal resting ECG doesn't rule out angina.
actions.why: New exertional chest pain earns an ECG today.

actions.label: Order lipids, HbA1c, kidney check
actions.text: Ordered: lipids, HbA1c, eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio.

options: Probable stable angina
Acute coronary syndrome: call 000 now
Stable blood pressure: script only
Chest wall (musculoskeletal) pain
Start antibiotics in case it's a chest infection
Explain the plan and check he's understood
Short-acting GTN spray, with clear instructions
Lipids, HbA1c and kidney check, and a CVD risk review
Increase his blood pressure tablet and recheck in a month
Prompt cardiology assessment for further testing
Renew his blood pressure medicine
Reassure: probably deconditioning; review in 12 months
Drive yourself to ED if it gets really bad
Take two paracetamol and lie down until it passes
Mention it at your next review if it's still there
000 if pain at rest, worsening, or lasting 10 minutes

extras.label: Also bill a GP chronic condition management plan (965) today
extras.why: GPCCMP items can't be co-claimed with a general attendance on the same day. Book the plan as its own visit.

src.t: MBS Online: GP chronic condition management plans

extras.label: Mark the HbA1c request 'established diabetes' so it's rebated
extras.why: He doesn't have diabetes. 66551 is for monitoring established diabetes; a diagnostic HbA1c in an asymptomatic high-risk patient is 66841, once in 12 months.

extras.label: Item 11714: 12-lead ECG, trace plus your clinical note (indication and interpretation)
extras.why: You did the ECG and read it to decide what happens next. Since 1 March 2026 that's 11714 for a GP, on top of the consult. Keep the ECG minutes out of the consult tier.
extras.whyNo: No ECG was done, so there's no ECG to bill.

src.t: MBS Online: ECG items 11707 and 11714 amended (1 March 2026)

extras.label: Item 11707 for the same ECG
extras.why: 11707 is a trace sent to a specialist or consultant physician for a formal report. You interpreted this one yourself: that's 11714.

src.t: MBS Online: ECG items 11707 and 11714 amended (1 March 2026)

pearl: The "just a script" consult is where angina likes to hide. Leave room for "anything else?", and if the answer is chest pain on exertion, the plan isn't "see you next year".

name: Graham
criticalWhy: Chest pain at rest in the waiting room. Every minute in the queue is heart muscle.
who: Back again. You saw him for a repeat script.
opening: "It's happening walking to the letterbox now. Had a bad one this morning just sitting down."

actions.label: How has the pain changed?
actions.text: Now with minimal effort, and twice at rest. This morning's lasted about 15 minutes.
actions.why: Pain at rest or on minimal effort is the change that makes this unstable.

actions.label: Any pain right now?
actions.text: Mild tightness now. Started about 20 minutes ago in the waiting room.
actions.why: Ongoing pain right now changes everything about the next ten minutes.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Scared it's a heart attack, like his brother. Hoping for "a stronger pill".

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "Isn't that enough?" Fair.

actions.label: Obs: BP, pulse, sats
actions.text: BP 150/90, HR 92, sats 96% on air. Pale and clammy.
actions.why: Obs tell you how sick he is right now and whether GTN is safe.

actions.label: 12-lead ECG
actions.text: ST depression in the lateral leads.
actions.why: The ECG is quick and changes the urgency, but it shouldn't delay calling the ambulance.

actions.label: Arrange an exercise stress test
actions.text: Booked for next month.
actions.why: Never stress test someone with possible unstable angina.

actions.label: Send a troponin to the lab
actions.text: Result in hours. He needs a hospital, not a courier.
actions.why: A community troponin delays transfer and doesn't change what he needs.

options: Reflux, worse after a heavy meal
Unstable angina (acute coronary syndrome)
Stable angina, now a bit more frequent
Anxiety about his brother's heart attack
Routine oxygen by mask, even though his sats are 96%
Aspirin 300 mg, chewed or dissolved (unless contraindicated)
Explain what's happening and why
GTN spray while waiting, watching his blood pressure
Send him home with a stronger tablet and rest
Book an outpatient exercise stress test next month
Call 000 for urgent ambulance transfer
Come back if it happens again this week
Let him wait in the car park for the ambulance
Stay with him, monitor, send a summary
He can drive himself to hospital if he's careful

pearl: Angina that's new, worse or happening at rest is an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise. Aspirin, ECG, ambulance, in whichever order gets them all done fastest.

extras.label: Item 11714: 12-lead ECG, trace plus your clinical note (indication and interpretation)
extras.why: You did the ECG and read it to decide what happens next. Since 1 March 2026 that's 11714 for a GP, on top of the consult. Keep the ECG minutes out of the consult tier.
extras.whyNo: No ECG was done, so there's no ECG to bill.

src.t: MBS Online: ECG items 11707 and 11714 amended (1 March 2026)

extras.label: Item 11707 for the same ECG
extras.why: 11707 is a trace sent to a specialist or consultant physician for a formal report. You interpreted this one yourself: that's 11714.

src.t: MBS Online: ECG items 11707 and 11714 amended (1 March 2026)

name: Maya
criticalWhy: A floppy, feverish toddler is time-critical. Seeing her last means she waited longest.
who: Here with her dad, Emeka. Usually a chatterbox.
opening: "She's been hot since last night. Now she just wants to lie on me."

actions.label: Fever story
actions.text: Fever since last night. Vomited twice. Refusing drinks; only one wet nappy today.

actions.label: Immunisations
actions.text: Up to date for her age.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: "She's never been like this." He wants her checked properly, and he's right to.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "She screamed when I touched her legs this morning. She never does that."
actions.why: Leg pain is an early warning sign of meningococcal sepsis in children.

actions.label: Obs: temp, heart rate, cap refill
actions.text: Temp 39.4°C, HR 170, capillary refill 4 seconds. Cold hands and feet.
actions.why: Cold peripheries and slow cap refill in a febrile child are early sepsis signs.

actions.label: Check her skin all over
actions.text: Several purple spots on her legs that don't fade when you press a glass on them.
actions.why: A non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

actions.label: Neck and alertness
actions.text: Drowsy and irritable when handled. Neck hard to assess.

actions.label: Urine dipstick
actions.text: Three minutes of coaxing, no sample. The clock didn't wait.
actions.why: A urine sample was never going to change the plan for this child.

actions.label: Attempt a lumbar puncture in the clinic
actions.text: Not possible here.
actions.why: Not a GP procedure, and it delays antibiotics and transfer.

options: Urinary tract infection
Gastroenteritis with dehydration
Suspected meningococcal sepsis
Viral illness with a high fever
Paracetamol, oral fluids and review first thing tomorrow
Oral antibiotics and home with Dad, review in 24 hours
Wait for a urine sample before deciding on antibiotics
Phone the receiving hospital and hand over
Explain to her dad what's happening and why
IV or IM antibiotics now, without delaying transfer
Call 000 for urgent transfer
Come back tomorrow if she's no better
Dad can drive her to ED if the traffic's OK
Stay with her until the ambulance arrives
Back to the waiting room until the ambulance comes

pearl: In a febrile child: leg pain, cold hands and feet and pale or mottled skin can come before the rash. Once there's a non-blanching rash, antibiotics and an ambulance shouldn't wait for anything.

name: Priya
who: Accountant. Two kids under five. Vegetarian.
opening: "I'm just exhausted. I figured it's work."

actions.label: Mood and sleep
actions.text: Mood fine, still enjoys things. Sleeps 7 hours. No snoring.

actions.label: Diet
actions.text: Vegetarian, eats a varied diet.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Wonders about her thyroid (her mum has hypothyroidism). Expects blood tests.

actions.label: "Being tired is normal with young kids."
actions.text: "Yeah, probably."
actions.why: Tiredness has causes. Hers was iron deficiency from heavy periods.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "Also... my periods have got really heavy. I'm flooding through pads overnight."
actions.why: Heavy periods were the cause, and she only mentioned them because you asked.

actions.label: Periods: tell me more
actions.text: Heavy for 7 days with clots, changing pads every 1 to 2 hours on heavy days. Regular cycle. No bleeding between periods or after sex.
actions.why: A bleeding history shapes both the diagnosis and whether she needs imaging.

actions.label: Obs and colour
actions.text: Pale. HR 96, BP 112/70.

actions.label: Pelvic examination (with consent)
actions.text: With consent: no masses, uterus feels normal size.

actions.label: Full blood count and ferritin
actions.text: Hb 98 g/L (low). Ferritin 6 µg/L (typical range for women roughly 30 to 300).
actions.why: The standard says to check FBC and ferritin routinely in heavy menstrual bleeding.

actions.label: Thyroid function
actions.text: TSH normal.

actions.label: Check B12, folate, vitamin D and a coeliac screen
actions.text: Ordered.
actions.why: Shotgun testing before the obvious cause (heavy periods) is checked. Coeliac is reasonable later if iron doesn't respond.

actions.label: Pregnancy test
actions.text: Negative.

options: Iron deficiency from heavy periods
Depression with low energy
Burnout from shift work
Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
Start iron replacement
Refer for gastroscopy and colonoscopy to find blood loss
Discuss treatments for the heavy bleeding
Pelvic ultrasound for everyone with heavy periods, regardless
Explain the plan and check she's understood
More red meat, an early night and review in 6 months
See you in a year for a recheck
Stop the iron straight away if your stools go dark
Nothing to worry about: it's very common
Sooner if breathless, faint or bleeding more

extras.label: Order TSH first (the lab adds free T4 only if TSH is abnormal)
extras.why: You don't bill this; the lab does. TSH is rebated as item 66716. Free T4/T3 (66719) is only rebated if the TSH is abnormal or a listed reason applies, so for a tired patient you request TSH and the lab does the rest.

extras.label: Also order vitamin D because she's tired
extras.why: Tiredness isn't a 66833 indication, so there's no rebate and Priya may get a bill.

extras.label: Item 35503 today, for the IUD discussion
extras.why: 35503 is the insertion itself. Talking through a hormonal IUD is part of today's consult; bill 35503 on the day it goes in.

pearl: "Tired all the time" in a menstruating woman: ask about periods, then check FBC and ferritin. The hormonal IUD is the most effective medical treatment for heavy bleeding when there's no significant pathology.

sources.t: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding Clinical Care Standard
Lifeblood: causes of iron deficiency anaemia

name: Tom
who: Apprentice carpenter. Started deadlifting last month.
opening: "Did deadlifts Saturday and my back's killing me. Can I get a scan and something strong?"

actions.label: Pain story
actions.text: Low back ache, worse bending. No pain down the legs.

actions.label: Bladder, bowel, saddle numbness
actions.text: No trouble passing urine, no bowel change, no numbness "down below".
actions.why: Cauda equina symptoms are the one thing you can't afford to skip in back pain.

actions.label: Fever, weight loss, cancer, injecting
actions.text: None.
actions.why: Screening for infection, malignancy and fracture is part of every back pain assessment.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks he's "slipped a disc". Worried he'll lose his apprenticeship. Expects an MRI and oxycodone.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "Nah, that's it."

actions.label: Leg neuro exam
actions.text: Normal power, reflexes and sensation.
actions.why: A focused neuro exam is how you show yourself there's no nerve compromise.

actions.label: Back exam
actions.text: Tender muscles either side of the spine. Bending forward limited by pain.

actions.label: Prescribe codeine for 2 weeks
actions.text: Script written.
actions.why: Opioids don't improve recovery from acute back pain and carry risks.

actions.label: Lumbar X-ray
actions.text: Normal. Which you could have predicted.
actions.why: Imaging wasn't indicated: no red flags.

actions.label: MRI request
actions.text: Without alerting features, imaging isn't recommended, and incidental disc findings can frighten people.
actions.why: An MRI without red flags tends to find things that aren't the problem.

options: Disc prolapse needing surgery
Non-specific low back pain
Cauda equina syndrome
Spinal stress fracture
Explain the plan and why no scan is needed
Review in 1 to 2 weeks if not improving
Simple pain relief to help him keep moving
Stay active and keep doing usual activities, modified as needed
A week of bed rest, then a gradual return to the gym
Oxycodone twice daily for two weeks to cover the pain
Order an MRI of the lumbar spine to check the discs
No need to come back: it always settles
Take more tablets if it hurts more
Come back if it's not gone in 6 months
Same day for bladder, bowel, saddle numbness or weak legs

pearl: Most acute back pain settles. Screen for red flags, examine, then sell activity. Bed rest is harmful and opioids are for carefully selected patients, lowest dose, shortest time.

sources.t: Low Back Pain Clinical Care Standard

name: June
criticalWhy: A head injury on an anticoagulant can bleed quietly. Seeing her last cost her hours.
who: Lives alone, gardens daily. Her daughter Eleni brought her in.
blurb: Fell last night. Daughter "a bit worried".
opening: "I'm fine, love. Eleni made me come."

actions.label: What happened?
actions.text: Tripped on a rug getting up to the toilet. Hit her head on the bedside table.
actions.why: A head strike changes this from a fall to a head injury.

actions.label: Medicines
actions.text: Apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Blood pressure tablet.
actions.why: Anticoagulation is the detail that makes this head injury urgent.

actions.label: Headache, vomiting, drowsiness
actions.text: Headache since. Vomited once this morning.
actions.why: Headache and vomiting after a head injury need asking about every time.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Worried she'll be "put in a home". Wants a quick check and to get back to her tomatoes.

actions.label: "Anything else?" (to Eleni too)
actions.doorknob: Eleni: "She's been asking me the same question over and over this morning."
actions.why: New repetitive questioning after a head injury is a worrying change.

actions.label: Obs
actions.text: BP 150/80, HR 88 irregular. Alert, but asks you the same thing twice.

actions.label: Head and neuro exam
actions.text: Bruise over the right temple. No focal weakness.

actions.label: Tell her to take tonight's apixaban as usual
actions.text: She says she will.
actions.why: Anticoagulants after a head injury need a CT first.

actions.label: Finger-prick glucose
actions.text: 6.1 mmol/L.

actions.label: Routine bloods
actions.text: Results tomorrow. Not much use today.
actions.why: Routine bloods don't answer the question that matters today: is she bleeding inside her head?

options: Stroke causing the fall
Urine infection causing confusion
Head injury on an anticoagulant: urgent CT
Simple mechanical fall, no injury
Carry on with apixaban as usual and review tomorrow
Observe her in the treatment room for an hour, then decide
Ice pack, simple pain relief and home with Eleni
Explain the plan to June and Eleni
Same-day transfer to ED for a CT head scan
000 if drowsier, confused, vomiting or worse headache
Watch her overnight at home and wake her hourly
Come back next week if she's still sore
Let her sleep it off and call in the morning

extras.label: Also bill a 75+ health assessment (701 to 707) today
extras.why: Today was an acute head injury, not a health assessment. You can only bill a health assessment you actually did; book one when she's well.

pearl: NICE suggests considering a CT head within 8 hours of injury for anyone on an anticoagulant, even with no other indication. Add vomiting and new repetitive questioning, and the decision makes itself.

name: Jayden
who: Aboriginal boy from a remote community. Here with his nan, Aunty Rose.
opening: Aunty Rose: "He's had a sore throat for two days and he's off his food."

actions.label: Symptoms
actions.text: Sore throat and fever. No cough.

actions.label: Rheumatic fever history
actions.text: His cousin has rheumatic heart disease. Jayden hasn't had rheumatic fever.
actions.why: Living in a high-risk setting, with family history, is what decides treatment.

actions.label: Ask about his school reading level
actions.text: Doing well, likes footy.
actions.why: Nice rapport, but not why he's here.

actions.label: Skin sores
actions.text: A few healing school sores on his legs.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Aunty Rose asks if he'll need "the needle every month" like his cousin. Hopes he's back at school soon.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "No, that's it."

actions.label: Throat and neck
actions.text: Red tonsils, tender neck glands.

actions.label: Heart and joints
actions.text: No murmur. No joint swelling.

actions.label: ASOT and anti-DNase B blood tests today
actions.text: Ordered. He cries at the needle.
actions.why: Not needed to treat a sore throat in a high-risk child. Blood tests come in if you suspect rheumatic fever itself.

actions.label: Throat swab
actions.text: Sent. In a high-risk setting, treatment shouldn't wait for it.

options: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) needing drainage
Viral sore throat: no treatment needed
High rheumatic fever risk: treat the throat
Acute rheumatic fever, already established
Explain to both, and answer the needle question honestly
Prescribe amoxicillin only if a rapid strep test is positive
Treat the skin sores as well
Symptom relief only: paracetamol, fluids and rest
Wait for the throat swab result before deciding
Penicillin now, as he's in a high-risk group
Back for sore joints, breathlessness, chest pain
Come back if he starts coughing
Only come back if it's still sore in a month
No need to come back: it's viral

extras.label: Also bill a 715 health assessment today
extras.why: A 715 is a full health assessment with set components and a 9-month gap rule. A sore-throat consult isn't one, however good. Offer to book one.

pearl: Where rheumatic fever is common, a sore throat or skin sore is a prevention opportunity. Treat with penicillin, treat the skin, and make sure follow-up is easy.
cu: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health

name: Mei
who: Primary school teacher. Last period 2 years ago.
opening: "The night sweats are wrecking my sleep. My friend says HRT changed her life."

actions.label: Symptoms
actions.text: About 10 flushes a day. Wakes drenched most nights.

actions.label: "Spotting is normal at your age."
actions.text: She seems relieved.
actions.why: Bleeding after menopause needs investigating for endometrial cancer.

actions.label: Past history
actions.text: No personal history of breast cancer or blood clots. Non-smoker.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Worried hormones cause cancer. Hoping to leave with a script today.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "Oh, I've had a bit of spotting the last couple of months. Probably nothing?"
actions.why: Bleeding after menopause needs investigating before MHT starts.

actions.label: Spotting: tell me more
actions.text: Light spotting three times in two months. No pain.
actions.why: Postmenopausal bleeding is a red flag in its own right.

actions.label: Speculum exam (with consent)
actions.text: Cervix looks normal. No obvious source of bleeding.

actions.label: FSH and oestradiol levels to confirm menopause
actions.text: Ordered.
actions.why: At 56 with typical symptoms, hormone levels add nothing. The bleeding is the issue.

actions.label: Write the MHT script now; investigate the bleeding later
actions.text: Script written.
actions.why: Starting hormones before investigating postmenopausal bleeding can mask an endometrial cancer.

options: Thyroid disease causing the flushes
Periods returning: normal at her age
Menopause symptoms plus bleeding to investigate
Menopause symptoms: start MHT today
Start oestrogen-only MHT today and review in 3 months
Explain the plan and check she's understood
Investigate the bleeding first (ultrasound, then gynae)
When MHT is appropriate: oestrogen plus progestogen
Start a low-dose combined pill to control the bleeding
Tell her spotting is normal for a year after menopause
Ignore the spotting: it's normal on MHT
Report any more bleeding; return for the results
Only come back if the flushes get worse
Come back in a year for a script review

pearl: MHT is the most effective treatment for hot flushes, but any unexplained vaginal bleeding gets investigated before it's prescribed. With a uterus, oestrogen always comes with a progestogen.

name: Sam
who: Works in hospitality. Uses they/them. Plays club rugby.
opening: "I just need something to help me sleep."

actions.label: Sleep
actions.text: Awake until 3am most nights for two months.

actions.label: Mood and interest
actions.text: Low most days. Stopped going to training. Eating less.

actions.label: "Everyone has bad patches. Try to get out more."
actions.text: "Yeah… I'll try."
actions.why: Minimising misses depression and suicide risk. Ask directly.

actions.label: Long talk on sleep hygiene and screens
actions.text: Sam nods politely.
actions.why: Sleep hygiene alone misses the depression and the suicidal thoughts.

actions.label: Ask directly about suicide
actions.text: "Sometimes I think everyone'd be better off without me." No plan. No previous attempts.
actions.why: Asking directly is safe, and people often won't volunteer it unless asked.

actions.label: Alcohol and drugs
actions.text: Drinking more on weekends.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks it's "just stress". Worried about being judged. Hoped for sleeping tablets.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "My housemate moved out last month. It's pretty quiet at home now."

actions.label: Mental state
actions.text: Flat, quiet, good eye contact. No signs of injury.

actions.label: Depression questionnaire
actions.text: Scores in the severe range.

actions.label: Thyroid, iron and vitamin D tests
actions.text: Ordered.
actions.why: Reasonable later, but not before you've asked about mood and safety.

options: Alcohol use disorder
Insomnia only: sleep hygiene
Depression with suicidal thoughts
Bipolar disorder, in a high phase
Book a review within days, not months
Make a safety plan together
Arrange psychological therapy
Explain the plan and check they've understood
Sleeping tablets for a month and a review in 3 months
Refer to a sleep clinic for an overnight study first
Crisis contacts: Lifeline 13 11 14, or 000 in an emergency
000, Lifeline or ED if the thoughts get stronger
Have a nightcap to help you get to sleep
Try to distract yourself and not think about it
Come back if you're still not sleeping in 3 months

pearl: "Can't sleep" is a common ticket of entry for depression. Ask about suicide directly and kindly; it doesn't plant the idea, and it may be the only way you find out.

extras.label: Also bill a mental health treatment plan (2700) because you arranged therapy
extras.why: A plan (2700) needs at least 20 minutes on the plan itself and its required components, with its own time if you also bill a 23. Arranging therapy in a standard consult isn't a plan. Book a long appointment for it, soon.

src.t: RACGP: MBS mental health item changes for GPs

name: Sam
criticalWhy: Someone at immediate risk sat in the waiting room the longest.
who: Back again, with their friend Jess. You saw Sam about sleep.
opening: Jess: "Sam sent me a message last night that really scared me."

actions.label: Ask directly about suicide
actions.text: "I've been thinking about it a lot. I looked up ways last night."
actions.why: You can't judge risk without asking directly.

actions.label: Access to means
actions.text: Has been saving up tablets at home.
actions.why: Access to means is one of the most modifiable risks.

actions.label: Ask Sam to sign a no-harm contract
actions.text: Sam signs it.
actions.why: No-harm contracts don't keep people safe and can give false reassurance.

actions.label: Who's around?
actions.text: Jess can stay with Sam today.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Sam is ashamed and frightened. Jess wants to know Sam will be safe tonight.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "I didn't tell you everything last time."

actions.label: Mental state
actions.text: Tearful, hopeless. Says they can't keep themselves safe right now.
actions.why: Whether they can stay safe right now decides where they go next.

actions.label: Routine bloods
actions.text: Not the priority right now.
actions.why: Bloods can wait. Safety can't.

options: Adjustment reaction with low ongoing risk
Depression with high, immediate suicide risk
Insomnia, made worse by stress
Sam isn't left alone: Jess stays until handover
Home tonight, with a review booked in a fortnight
Urgent same-day crisis assessment
Explain what happens next, to Sam and Jess
Increase the antidepressant dose and review next week
Reduce access to means (the saved tablets)
Book a fortnightly review to monitor
000 if Sam can't stay safe before assessment
Leave it to Sam to decide what happens next
See how tonight goes and call in the morning

pearl: When someone can't keep themselves safe, the plan is same-day crisis care, someone with them, and less access to means. Ask, act, and hand over warmly.

name: Abdi
who: Arrived in Australia 4 months ago as a refugee. Somali speaker. Just started work as a delivery driver.
opening: (In Somali, gesturing to a form) "Cough... and the form, for my job."

actions.label: Book a phone interpreter (TIS)
actions.text: A Somali interpreter joins. Now you can actually take a history.

actions.label: Cough details
actions.text: Cough for 6 weeks. Some blood-streaked sputum.
actions.why: A cough over three weeks, especially with blood, is a TB flag.

actions.label: Detailed travel history for the last holiday
actions.text: No holidays. Hasn't left Australia since arriving.
actions.why: His country of birth and arrival matter; holiday plans don't.

actions.label: Fevers, sweats, weight
actions.text: Night sweats. Lost about 6 kg.
actions.why: Night sweats and weight loss complete the TB picture.

actions.label: Who lives with you?
actions.text: His wife and three children.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Worried he'll lose his new job. Expects cough medicine and a signed form.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.doorknob: "My cousin had TB in the camp."
actions.why: A known TB contact raises the stakes considerably.

actions.label: Chest and temperature
actions.text: Crackles at the right upper chest. Temp 37.8°C.

actions.label: Start amoxicillin now and review in a week
actions.text: Script written.
actions.why: Antibiotics don't treat TB and can delay the diagnosis.

actions.label: Chest X-ray and sputum for TB
actions.text: Requested: chest X-ray and sputum samples for TB testing.
actions.why: Chest X-ray and sputum are the first tests for suspected lung TB.

options: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
Viral bronchitis
Asthma, triggered by work dust
Reflux-related cough
Cough syrup, and sign the fit-for-work form today
Explain through the interpreter; check understanding
Chest X-ray and sputum tests for TB
Contact the TB clinic urgently: care is free
A week of amoxicillin, then review if still coughing
Keep working and return if it gets worse
Urgently if you cough more blood or get breathless
Come back if the cough lasts another 6 weeks
No need to come back once the form's done

actions.text: The support worker nods.

actions.label: Order a CT brain
actions.text: Requested.

Urgent help if fainting with chest pain or exertion
Come back if the anxiety gets worse
Cut back on fluids to stop the palpitations

pearl: ‘Anxiety’ isn't a diagnosis of exclusion you reach by not examining. A cuff, a clock and 10 minutes standing found the answer.

sources.t: Sheldon RS et al. HRS consensus on POTS. Heart Rhythm 2015

name: Lorraine
criticalWhy: A woman with diabetes and ‘indigestion’, sweating in the waiting room, may be having a heart attack.
who: Type 2 diabetes. Reception wrote: ‘indigestion, probably stress, not urgent’.
opening: "I feel silly. It's just indigestion, and I'm so tired."

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks it's the curry. Doesn't want a fuss.

actions.label: Characterise it: when, where, what with
actions.text: Started 2 hours ago. Heavy feeling high in the belly, aching jaw and between the shoulders. Nauseous, vomited once.
actions.why: Atypical sites and nausea are common heart attack symptoms in women and people with diabetes.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "I'm sweating, which is odd."

actions.label: Ask what she had for lunch
actions.text: A curry.
actions.why: Diet doesn't explain sweating and jaw pain.

actions.label: "It's probably just stress. Busy week?"
actions.text: "I suppose so…" She looks greyer.
actions.why: A heart attack without chest pain is common in women and people with diabetes. ECG first.

actions.label: Pulse, BP, sats, look at her
actions.text: Grey and clammy. Pulse 104, BP 152/92, sats 96%.

actions.label: ECG
actions.text: ST depression V4–V6.
actions.why: Any unexplained ‘indigestion’ in a high-risk patient earns an ECG within 10 minutes.

actions.label: Antacid trial and review tomorrow
actions.text: Given.
actions.why: This delays a time-critical diagnosis.

options: Gallstones
Reflux (gastro-oesophageal reflux)
Acute coronary syndrome: call 000
Anxiety and stress
Let her drive home and come back if worse
Explain what's happening and check she's understood
Monitor her and send the ECG with her
Trial a PPI and review in the morning
Aspirin 300 mg to chew (if not allergic)
Call 000
She can wait in the waiting room
Book an echo for next week
Stay with her until the ambulance arrives
Call her tomorrow to check in

pearl: About 1 in 3 heart attacks arrive without chest pain, more often in women, older people and people with diabetes. Reception's ‘probably stress’ is a label, not a triage.

sources.t: Mehta LS et al. Acute MI in women: AHA scientific statement. Circulation 2016

name: Kezia
who: Uni student. Seen 4 times in 3 years for period pain. Told ‘normal’ and to take the pill.
opening: "Everyone says periods hurt. But I'm missing uni every month."

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Scared she's imagining it. Wants a name for it and to know about fertility.

actions.label: Pain pattern, sex, bowels, bladder
actions.text: Pain starts before bleeding, 9/10. Pain with deep sex, painful bowel motions during periods.
actions.why: Dysmenorrhoea plus deep dyspareunia and dyschezia strongly suggest endometriosis.

actions.label: Impact: work, study, relationships
actions.text: Misses 2–3 days of uni a month. Avoids sex.
actions.why: Impact on life matters more than how ‘normal’ the bleeding looks.

actions.label: "Dr Google isn't a medical degree."
actions.text: "I just read about endometriosis…"
actions.why: Her research was right. Explore what worried her instead of shutting it down.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "My sister has endometriosis."

actions.label: "Period pain is normal. Some women just feel it more."
actions.text: She goes quiet. "OK. Sorry."
actions.why: Pain that stops life isn't normal. This line is why endometriosis takes 6.5 years to diagnose.

actions.label: Pelvic exam: trauma-informed consent first
actions.text: Explained; she agreed and knew she could stop. Tender, fixed retroverted uterus; nodularity behind the cervix.
actions.why: Explain, ask, offer a chaperone and the right to stop.

actions.label: Pregnancy test and STI screen
actions.text: Negative.

actions.label: CA-125 blood test
actions.text: Ordered.
actions.why: Not a test for endometriosis. It's often raised by benign conditions.

actions.label: Pelvic ultrasound (ideally a specialised endometriosis scan)
actions.text: Booked.
actions.why: A normal standard ultrasound doesn't rule out endometriosis.

options: Probable endometriosis
Normal period pain
IBS
Pelvic inflammatory disease
Laparoscopy is needed before any treatment starts
Regular NSAIDs starting before the period
Tell her period pain is normal and to toughen up
Refer to a gynaecologist who treats endometriosis
Hormonal treatment, e.g. a continuous pill
Pelvic floor physio and pain support
Explain, believe her, and check she's understood
Only come back if the bleeding stops completely
Review in 3 months; ED for sudden pain or fever
No follow-up needed: just stay on the pill
Come back when you want to try for a baby

pearl: Average diagnostic delay in Australia is 6.5 years. Pain that stops life isn't normal, and a clinical diagnosis lets treatment start before surgery.

name: Malcolm
who: Notes say ‘chronic back pain, frequent attender’. Third visit this month.
opening: "Sorry, doc. The back again. Just need something stronger."

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks he's a nuisance. Hasn't mentioned some things because ‘you're busy’.

actions.label: "Your bloods last year were normal."
actions.text: He nods, reassured.
actions.why: Old results don't explain new symptoms.

actions.label: Red flags: night pain, weight, bladder, bowels, legs
actions.text: Pain worse at night, lying down. Lost 6 kg. Legs feel heavy; a bit unsteady on the stairs.
actions.why: New features in a ‘known’ back pain are the signal.

actions.label: "Let's not go down a rabbit hole. It's your usual back."
actions.text: "Right. Sorry, doc."
actions.why: ‘Frequent attender’ thinking misses new red flags.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "Getting up to wee a lot. Never had my prostate checked."

actions.label: Leg neuro exam and spine
actions.text: Brisk knee reflexes, upgoing toes, mild weakness in both legs. Tender mid-thoracic spine.
actions.why: Upper motor neurone signs mean the problem is in the spinal cord.

actions.label: PSA, blood count, calcium, kidney function
actions.text: PSA 240. Calcium 2.8.

actions.label: Increase his opioid and review in 4 weeks
actions.text: Done.
actions.why: Stronger painkillers mask a spinal emergency.

actions.label: Lumbar X-ray
actions.text: Mild wear and tear.
actions.why: X-rays miss early spread and cord problems. It's falsely reassuring.

options: Chronic mechanical back pain flaring
Cancer pressing on the spinal cord
Opioid-seeking behaviour
Muscle strain from the garden
Same-day emergency whole-spine MRI
Physiotherapy referral for core strengthening
Increase his pain relief and review in 4 weeks
Lie flat and avoid weight bearing until assessed
Explain what's suspected, and check he's understood
Discuss dexamethasone with the on-call team
Go now; 000 if legs weaken or he can't wee
Physio first, then review
Rest at home and review in a week
Come back next week if no better

pearl: ‘Frequent attender’ is a label that stops thinking. A patient who keeps coming back is telling you the first answer didn't fit.

sources.t: NICE NG234: Spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression

name: Beryl
who: Widowed. Lives alone. Loves a chat. Long appointments booked as short ones.
opening: "Oh, it's lovely to see you. Now, did I tell you about my granddaughter's wedding? The flowers were…"

actions.label: Let her tell the whole wedding story
actions.text: The flowers, the cousins, the cake, the caterer's divorce. Twelve minutes in, you know nothing medical.
actions.why: Warmth matters, but you need to steer, kindly.

actions.label: Set the agenda: "What would you like to sort out today?"
actions.text: "Well… my ankles are puffy and I'm puffed on the stairs. But it's nothing."
actions.why: Agenda-setting early saves the consult and finds the real problem.

actions.label: Gently refocus: "Can I stop you there? I want to hear about your breathing"
actions.text: She laughs. "Sorry, love, I do go on."
actions.why: Kind interruption, naming why, keeps rapport and time.

actions.label: Breathlessness: lying flat, at night, how far she can walk
actions.text: Sleeps on 3 pillows. Wakes gasping some nights. Can't walk to the letterbox without stopping.
actions.why: Orthopnoea and night breathlessness point to heart failure.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Worried she'll be ‘put in a home’. Wants to stay independent.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "My legs are like tree trunks by the evening."

actions.label: Heart, lungs, ankles, JVP, weight
actions.text: Crackles at both bases. Pitting oedema to the knees. JVP raised. Weight up 4 kg in a month.

actions.label: ECG
actions.text: Atrial fibrillation, rate 104. New.
actions.why: New AF can tip someone into heart failure.

actions.label: NT-proBNP, kidney function, electrolytes, FBC, TSH
actions.text: NT-proBNP very high. eGFR 48. Potassium normal.

actions.label: Look at the wedding photos on her phone
actions.text: They're lovely.
actions.why: Rapport is good. Three minutes of photos isn't.

options: New heart failure with atrial fibrillation
Chest infection
Loneliness and low mood
Dependent ankle oedema from age
Explain the plan and check she's understood
Anticoagulation discussion for the new AF
Echocardiogram and cardiology referral
Book her next visit as a long appointment
Tell her to cut out salt and come back if worse
Compression stockings only, review in 3 months
Start a diuretic and review in a few days
Rate control for the AF
Come back if the ankles stay puffy for another month
Call 000 if breathless at rest or chest pain; weigh daily
Nothing to worry about at her age
Put her feet up and see how she goes

pearl: Ramblers often bury the lead. Set the agenda early, interrupt kindly, and book longer next time.

name: Craig
criticalWhy: An aggressive, sweaty man with type 1 diabetes may be hypoglycaemic. Leaving him waiting is dangerous.
who: Type 1 diabetes. Reception says he swore at them and ‘smells of alcohol’.
opening: "I've been waiting forty bloody minutes! Just give me my script!" He's sweaty and slurring.

actions.label: Call security and ask him to leave
actions.text: He knocks over a chair on the way out. Collapses in the car park.
actions.why: Aggression plus slurring in a person with diabetes is hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise.

actions.label: Stay calm, keep a safe distance, speak slowly
actions.text: "Sorry… I feel weird."
actions.why: De-escalate first: calm voice, open posture, exit route.

actions.label: Finger-prick blood glucose
actions.text: 2.1 mmol/L.
actions.why: Check the sugar in anyone with diabetes who's confused, aggressive or ‘drunk’.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: After glucose: embarrassed. Skipped lunch, extra insulin for a big breakfast. Scared about his licence.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "I've had a few lows lately and didn't feel them coming."

actions.label: Breathalyse him
actions.why: The ‘alcohol’ smell was a label. Checking glucose first matters more.

actions.label: Explain the waiting-room rules firmly
actions.text: He shouts louder.
actions.why: Arguing escalates. Safety first, then talk.

options: Alcohol intoxication
Stroke
Personality disorder
Hypoglycaemia, with reduced awareness of lows
Send him home to sleep it off
Driving: no driving until reviewed, as per fitness-to-drive standards
Explain what happened, without judgement
Fast-acting glucose by mouth, then a longer-acting carb
Recheck glucose in 15 minutes
Ban him from the practice
Review insulin doses and hypo awareness
No need to come back once he's eaten
Only come back if he has another episode
Come back next month to talk about the anger
Glucagon for family; diabetes team review; don't drive today

pearl: Anger can be a symptom. Hypos, head injuries, pain and delirium all look like ‘bad behaviour’. Check the glucose.

name: Mia
who: Booked a 10-minute appointment for ‘a medical certificate’.
opening: She sits down and bursts into tears. "Sorry, sorry. I just need a certificate."

actions.label: Write the certificate and move on
actions.text: She takes it and leaves, still crying.
actions.why: The certificate wasn't the reason she came.

actions.label: Pause, offer tissues: "Take your time. What's happened?"
actions.text: "I lost the baby last week. Eight weeks. No one at work knew."
actions.why: Silence and acknowledgement come before questions.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks it was her fault for going to the gym. Wants to know if she can try again.

actions.label: Bleeding, pain, fever, discharge since
actions.text: Bleeding now light. No fever. Mild cramps.
actions.why: Check for retained tissue or infection.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "My partner won't talk about it."

actions.label: Mood, sleep and support
actions.text: Not sleeping. Crying daily. No thoughts of self-harm.

actions.label: Temperature, pulse, abdomen
actions.text: Normal.

actions.label: "At least it was early. You can try again."
actions.text: She goes quiet and looks at the floor.
actions.why: Minimising early loss hurts. Name it as a real loss.

options: Grief after early miscarriage, recovering physically
Retained products with infection
Postnatal depression
Adjustment disorder needing medication
Explain what's normal now, and check she's understood
The certificate, worded as she prefers
Pregnancy loss support (e.g. Pink Elephants)
Start an antidepressant today
Follow-up in 1–2 weeks, partner welcome
Reassure her it wasn't caused by the gym
Advise waiting 6 months before trying again
Only come back when you're pregnant again
ED for heavy bleeding, fever or severe pain; call if mood dips
Come back if you're still sad in 6 months
No need to come back: it's very common

pearl: Tears at the start mean the booking reason isn't the real reason. Pause, acknowledge, then ask.

name: Stavros
who: Retired builder. Brings a typed list about his bowels.
opening: "It's my bowels, doctor. Monday hard, Tuesday nothing, Wednesday…" He keeps going back to Monday.

actions.label: Go through his bowel diary day by day
actions.text: Monday again. Then Monday's dinner. Then back to Monday.
actions.why: Perseveration burns time. Summarise and move him on.

actions.label: Summarise and redirect: "So it's changed. Let me ask about other things"
actions.text: "Yes, changed. Since about March."
actions.why: Summarising shows you've heard, and lets you steer.

actions.label: Red flags: blood, weight, appetite, family history
actions.text: Dark blood mixed in. Lost 6 kg without trying. Brother had bowel cancer at 60.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Thinks it's ‘bad fibre’. Quietly scared because of his brother.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "I'm so tired lately."

actions.label: Abdominal and rectal exam (with consent)
actions.text: Abdomen soft. Dark blood on the glove; no mass felt.

actions.label: FBC, iron studies, kidney and liver tests
actions.text: Haemoglobin 98, ferritin 6.

actions.label: Send a bowel screening (FIT) kit
actions.text: Kit given.
actions.why: Screening kits are for people without symptoms. He needs a colonoscopy.

actions.label: Prescribe laxatives and finish
actions.text: He's pleased.
actions.why: Treating constipation misses the bleeding, weight loss and anaemia.

options: Suspected bowel cancer
Irritable bowel syndrome
Haemorrhoids
Constipation from low fibre
Explain the concern honestly, and check understanding
Urgent colonoscopy referral
Ask a family member to come next time, if he'd like
Start iron replacement
Fibre supplement and review in 3 months
Bowel screening kit and wait for the result
No need to come back after the kit
Come back next year for his check-up
Back sooner for heavy bleeding, pain or fainting
Come back if the diary doesn't improve

pearl: A patient stuck on one detail can still have a serious story underneath. Summarise, redirect, and ask the red-flag questions.

sources.t: Cancer Council: optimal care pathway for colorectal cancer

name: Jules
who: Graphic designer. Brought a list on their phone.
opening: "OK, I've got seven things. Number one: my knee clicks."

actions.label: Work through all seven, in their order
actions.text: Knee, ingrown toenail, dandruff, a script, travel vaccines, a mole, eye floaters.
actions.why: You'll run out of time before the important ones.

actions.label: "Let's hear the whole list, then pick the most important today"
actions.text: Reads them out. Pauses at number six: "A mole on my back's changed. My partner noticed."
actions.why: Hear the whole list first, then prioritise together.

actions.label: History of the mole: change, itch, bleeding
actions.text: Darker and bigger over 3 months. Bled once.

actions.label: Examine the mole with a dermatoscope
actions.text: 8 mm, asymmetric, two colours, irregular border.
actions.why: Changing pigmented lesion: think melanoma.

actions.label: Floaters: new? flashes? shadow?
actions.text: Had them for years. No change, no flashes.
actions.why: Quickly rule out the other possibly urgent item.

actions.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
actions.text: Mostly worried about the knee, for running. Didn't think the mole mattered.

actions.label: "Anything else?"
actions.text: "That's everything. It's all on the list!"

actions.label: Full knee examination
actions.text: Normal. Some clicking.
actions.why: Fine for another day. The mole is what matters today.

options: Seborrhoeic keratosis
Benign mole: reassure
Suspicious lesion: possible melanoma
Dysplastic naevus: watch
Freeze the mole today
Photograph and recheck in 6 months
Excision biopsy with a narrow margin, soon
Book another appointment for the rest of the list
Explain why the mole comes first today
Shave off the darkest part for testing
Only come back for the knee
No need to come back for results
Results within a week; sooner if it bleeds or grows
Come back next year for a skin check

pearl: With a list, hear the whole thing first and prioritise together. The thing they mention last is often the one that matters.
